articles.headline: Treasury Designates Iranian 'Shadow Banking' Network in Latest Sanctions Round
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026, targeting a vast 'shadow banking' system. This action is part of Operation Economic Outcast, which aims to disrupt financial channels used by Iran to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terrorism.

The sanctions specifically target more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. These entities are accused of facilitating billions of dollars in transactions through the international financial system, primarily operating out of Dubai, Turkey, and Hong Kong.

According to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Iran's economy is under severe pressure, forcing its leadership to increasingly rely on illicit financial networks. Washington has vowed to continue dismantling these networks to further isolate Iran from the global economy.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba on November 20, 2026. This action follows a previous round of sanctions under Operation Economic Outcast, which targets individuals involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and supporting designated entities.

The Iran designations are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt networks that enable the Iranian regime's illicit activities. The specific details of the newly designated entities were not immediately released but are expected to target further elements of Iran's financial infrastructure.

Concurrently, OFAC published new FAQs concerning Cuba, providing guidance and clarification on existing sanctions and authorized transactions. These updates aim to assist individuals and entities in complying with U.S. sanctions programs related to Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 19, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global criminal networks that pose a threat to national security and financial stability.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Illicit Drugs General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions related to illicit drug interdiction and enforcement efforts. This license aims to facilitate legitimate activities while maintaining pressure on illicit drug networks.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). These revisions provide additional guidance and clarify the scope of authorized activities under the existing Russia sanctions program, reflecting ongoing adjustments to address evolving geopolitical circumstances.

articles.headline: Treasury Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of a broader strategy to combat global terrorism and disrupt the financial networks that support terrorist organizations.

The specific individuals and entities targeted by these designations were not immediately detailed in the announcement but are expected to be those identified as providing material support, financial services, or other forms of aid to designated terrorist groups.

These designations aim to isolate the targeted individuals and entities from the international financial system, preventing them from accessing resources that could be used to plan or carry out terrorist acts.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a joint announcement on November 13, 2026, detailing new designations under both its counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. This coordinated action highlights the interconnectedness of illicit networks and the U.S. government's comprehensive approach to combating them.

The designations target individuals and entities identified as playing roles in both drug trafficking and terrorist financing, aiming to disrupt their ability to operate and generate funds for their illicit activities.

These actions reinforce the U.S. commitment to protecting the international financial system from abuse by criminal and terrorist organizations, emphasizing the importance of vigilance and robust compliance measures.

The designations target individuals and entities involved in various sectors that support the Iranian government, including those linked to its illicit financial networks, procurement efforts, or support for regional proxies.
These measures aim to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and limit its capacity to engage in activities deemed contrary to U.S. national security interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba Determination

These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating sophisticated criminal enterprises that exploit technology and operate across borders.

In addition to these designations, OFAC also issued new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures are part of the ongoing implementation of U.S. policy towards Cuba, aiming to address specific concerns while providing clarity on permissible activities.

The designations against cyber actors and transnational criminal organizations aim to disrupt their financial infrastructure and prevent them from engaging in activities such as ransomware attacks, fraud, and other illicit schemes.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

body: Tributes have flooded in for the 38-year-old Australian who is survived by his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter.

articles.headline: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
body: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.

articles.headline: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
body: The headquarters of Halk TV were raided last month, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed critical of the government.

articles.headline: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
body: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.

articles.headline: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
body: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

articles.headline: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
body: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.

articles.headline: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
body: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.

articles.headline: Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
body: Hundreds of thousands of people were without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

articles.headline: 'It's impossible': Spain's young people on housing ahead of Sunday's election
body: Europe correspondent Nick Beake speaks to one couple kept apart by high rents in Valencia.

articles.headline: Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats
body: Marvin Reuter is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

articles.headline: Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
body: Hundreds of thousands have been affected by storms in the country as the Thanksgiving holiday weekend begins.

articles.headline: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
body: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?

articles.headline: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
body: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.

articles.headline: A clinic is offering to reassess ADHD and autism diagnoses - and hundreds of people are interested
body: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
